-------

1. Use the `Adult Census Income` dataset.  We will predict the income (whether or not it is more than 50k or not) of an adult. Import the dataset.  Partition the data into 80% training and 20% testing.  


```{r import-and-split}
# Keep adult_census.csv in the same folder as this R Markdown file.
# The question marks in this file represent missing values.
adult <- read_csv("adult_census.csv", na = c("", "NA", "?"))
rows_before <- nrow(adult)
colSums(is.na(adult))

df <- adult %>%
  rename(target = income) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor),
         target = factor(target, levels = c("<=50K", ">50K")))

set.seed(421)
splitIndex <- createDataPartition(df$target, p = .80, list = FALSE)
df_train <- df[splitIndex, ]
df_test <- df[-splitIndex, ]

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Dataset = c("Original", "After removing missing rows", "Training", "Testing"),
  Records = c(rows_before, nrow(df), nrow(df_train), nrow(df_test))
))
table(df$target)
```

I removed `r rows_before - nrow(df)` records containing missing values,
leaving `r nrow(df)` complete records. The target is a factor with two
categories: `<=50K` and `>50K`. The positive class is `>50K`.
The split uses about 80% for training and 20% for testing, with similar
income proportions in each set. All eight models use this same split.


2. Practice Decision Tree.  Do the follows:

  - Use `rpart` package, create a decision tree with maximum depth of 3. 
  
  - Calculate the accuracy of the model on the testing data. Notice that the positive outcome here is not `1` but `>50K` or `<50K`. 
  
  - Plot the tree
  
  - Plot the variable importance by the tree
  

```{r first-decision-tree}
tree_model <- rpart(target ~ ., data = df_train, method = "class",
                    control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 3))

tree_pred <- predict(tree_model, df_test, type = "class")
tree_cm <- confusionMatrix(data = tree_pred, reference = df_test$target,
                           positive = ">50K")
tree_cm
tree_cm$overall["Accuracy"]
```

The first decision tree has testing accuracy of
**`r round(100 * tree_cm$overall["Accuracy"], 2)`%**.

```{r plot-decision-tree}
rpart.plot(tree_model, main = "Adult income: decision tree with maximum depth 3",
           extra = 104, fallen.leaves = TRUE, faclen = 3, varlen = 0, cex = .65)
```

```{r tree-importance}
tree_importance <- sort(tree_model$variable.importance, decreasing = TRUE)
par(mar = c(10, 5, 5, 2))
barplot(tree_importance, las = 2, cex.names = .8, col = "steelblue",
        main = "Variable importance: depth-3 decision tree", cex.main = .9,
        ylab = "Importance")
```

Category names in the tree are abbreviated to fit the figure.
The tree uses a series of splits to classify income. A larger importance
value means a variable contributes more to this tree's splits; it does
not show that the variable causes higher income.


3. Create 3 more trees and compare the testing accuracy of these trees, which tree give the highest testing accuracy.


```{r three-more-trees}
# A smaller cp permits additional splits in the three deeper trees.
tree_2 <- rpart(target ~ ., data = df_train, method = "class",
               control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 5, cp = .001))
tree_3 <- rpart(target ~ ., data = df_train, method = "class",
               control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 7, cp = .001))
tree_4 <- rpart(target ~ ., data = df_train, method = "class",
               control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 10, cp = .001))

tree_2_cm <- confusionMatrix(predict(tree_2, df_test, type = "class"),
                             df_test$target, positive = ">50K")
tree_3_cm <- confusionMatrix(predict(tree_3, df_test, type = "class"),
                             df_test$target, positive = ">50K")
tree_4_cm <- confusionMatrix(predict(tree_4, df_test, type = "class"),
                             df_test$target, positive = ">50K")

tree_results <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Tree 1", "Tree 2", "Tree 3", "Tree 4"),
  Maximum_depth = c(3, 5, 7, 10),
  cp = c(.01, .001, .001, .001),
  Accuracy = c(tree_cm$overall["Accuracy"], tree_2_cm$overall["Accuracy"],
               tree_3_cm$overall["Accuracy"], tree_4_cm$overall["Accuracy"]),
  row.names = NULL
)
knitr::kable(tree_results, digits = 4)

best_trees <- tree_results %>% filter(Accuracy == max(Accuracy))
best_trees
```

The highest tree testing accuracy is
**`r round(100 * max(tree_results$Accuracy), 2)`%**, achieved by
**`r paste(best_trees$Model, collapse = ", ")`**.
Maximum depth limits the number of splitting levels. The complexity
parameter `cp` controls how much a proposed split must improve the fit;
a smaller value permits more splits. The table records both settings.


4. Practice Random Forest.  Do the follows: 

  - Use `randomForest` package, create a random forest of 1000 trees. 
  
  - Calculate the accuracy of the model on the testing data. 
  
  - Plot the variable importance by the forest


```{r first-random-forest}
set.seed(421)
forest_model <- randomForest(target ~ ., data = df_train, ntree = 1000)

forest_pred <- predict(forest_model, df_test, type = "class")
forest_cm <- confusionMatrix(data = forest_pred, reference = df_test$target,
                             positive = ">50K")
forest_cm
forest_cm$overall["Accuracy"]
```

The random forest with 1,000 trees has testing accuracy of
**`r round(100 * forest_cm$overall["Accuracy"], 2)`%**.

```{r forest-importance}
varImpPlot(forest_model, type = 2,
           main = "Variable importance: random forest with 1,000 trees")
```

The forest combines predictions from many trees using a majority vote.
The importance plot uses Mean Decrease Gini, which summarizes how much
each predictor helps separate classes across the forest's splits.
These scores describe predictive use, not causal effects.


5. Create 3 more forests and compare the testing accuracy of these forests, which forest give the highest testing accuracy.


```{r three-more-forests}
# Change the number of trees while keeping the other settings the same.
set.seed(421)
forest_2 <- randomForest(target ~ ., data = df_train, ntree = 100)
set.seed(421)
forest_3 <- randomForest(target ~ ., data = df_train, ntree = 500)
set.seed(421)
forest_4 <- randomForest(target ~ ., data = df_train, ntree = 1500)

forest_2_cm <- confusionMatrix(predict(forest_2, df_test, type = "class"),
                               df_test$target, positive = ">50K")
forest_3_cm <- confusionMatrix(predict(forest_3, df_test, type = "class"),
                               df_test$target, positive = ">50K")
forest_4_cm <- confusionMatrix(predict(forest_4, df_test, type = "class"),
                               df_test$target, positive = ">50K")

forest_results <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Forest 1", "Forest 2", "Forest 3", "Forest 4"),
  Trees = c(1000, 100, 500, 1500),
  Accuracy = c(forest_cm$overall["Accuracy"], forest_2_cm$overall["Accuracy"],
               forest_3_cm$overall["Accuracy"], forest_4_cm$overall["Accuracy"]),
  row.names = NULL
)
knitr::kable(forest_results, digits = 4)

best_forests <- forest_results %>% filter(Accuracy == max(Accuracy))
best_forests
```

The highest forest testing accuracy is
**`r round(100 * max(forest_results$Accuracy), 2)`%**, achieved by
**`r paste(paste0(best_forests$Model, " (", best_forests$Trees, " trees)"), collapse = ", ")`**.
Adding more trees does not guarantee a higher score on this particular test set.


6. What is the best model (in term of testing accuracy) among all models (including trees and forests) you have trained?



```{r compare-all-models}
all_results <- bind_rows(
  tree_results %>% select(Model, Accuracy),
  forest_results %>% select(Model, Accuracy)
) %>% arrange(desc(Accuracy))

knitr::kable(all_results, digits = 4)
best_models <- all_results %>% filter(Accuracy == max(Accuracy))

ggplot(all_results, aes(x = reorder(Model, Accuracy), y = Accuracy)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(Accuracy, accuracy = .01)),
            hjust = -.1, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent,
                     limits = c(0, 1), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .02))) +
  labs(title = "Testing accuracy of all eight income models",
       x = "Model", y = "Testing accuracy",
       caption = "Source: Adult Census Income data; the same 20% test set is used for all models.") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The best model on this testing split is
**`r paste(best_models$Model, collapse = ", ")`**, with accuracy of
**`r round(100 * max(all_results$Accuracy), 2)`%**.
For context, always predicting the majority income class on the test set
would have accuracy of **`r round(100 * tree_cm$overall["AccuracyNull"], 2)`%**.

This assignment asks us to compare models by testing accuracy. Because
this same test set also helps choose the winning model, its winning score
may be optimistic as an estimate of future performance. A separate final
holdout set would be useful for evaluating a model selected this way.
